title: Seen and Silenced: How Georgia Turned a Russian-Sourced Surveillance System Against Its Own Protesters
summary:
Since 2013, Georgia's Interior Ministry has operated Polyface, a facial recognition system supplied by sanctioned Moscow-based company Papillon AO, whose underlying algorithm was developed by a Novosibirsk firm backed by Russian state capital. Following disputed elections in October 2024, the system was deployed against hundreds of thousands of demonstrators. The documented enforcement mechanism is fines — and it is working: protesters describe changing their behavior to avoid cameras.

---
body:
Georgia's Ministry of Internal Affairs has been running Polyface since 2013. The system — a facial recognition platform supplied by Papillon AO, a Moscow-based company now sanctioned by the United States, Switzerland, Ukraine, and Japan — sits at the center of a surveillance infrastructure that has been used, since November 2024, against Georgians protesting alleged election fraud and their government's suspension of EU accession talks.

The protests began after parliamentary elections in October 2024 that many observers called fraudulent. They have not stopped. A full 580 days of daily demonstrations have followed, with over 486 people detained and 282 documented abuse cases in the initial months, according to AlgorithmWatch's investigation published June 27, 2026.

The facial recognition system runs three operational modes: automated identification through continuous scanning of live camera feeds; operator-directed search, in which a human controller manually targets a camera at an individual for real-time matching; and watchlist alerts, which flag pre-loaded individuals automatically. Polyface draws on Georgia's "Unified Information Bank" — a civil registry containing photographs of citizens — and can cross-reference social media images.

Papillon AO received a perpetual license to operate in Georgia in October 2024 — the same month as the disputed elections. The timing does not establish causation, but it establishes sequence.

The algorithm embedded in Polyface was developed not by Papillon AO but by 3DiVi, a company based in Novosibirsk and backed by a Russian state venture capital fund. The supply chain for Georgia's biometric enforcement infrastructure runs from a Russian state-adjacent algorithm vendor to a sanctioned Russian integrator to Georgia's own government.

### The Russian intelligence question

AlgorithmWatch's reporting does not establish a direct, documented contractual link between Papillon AO and Russia's Federal Security Service (the FSB). What it does establish is the legal framework that governs any Russian company: under Russian law, companies are obligated to cooperate with Russian security services when compelled.

Eto Buziashvili, a researcher at the Atlantic Council's Digital Forensic Research Lab, has described Papillon as "a core part of the Russian security infrastructure." That characterization is an analytical assessment, not a documented chain of command. What Buziashvili does say, on the record, is that Russian-controlled access to Georgian biometric data poses a distinct national security threat: the potential for "integrity attacks" and the intelligence profiling of Georgian citizens and institutional actors.

Georgia's Interior Ministry holds the biometric records. Papillon AO built and maintains the system that processes them.

### The chilling mechanism

The system's visible effect is not mass arrest. It is fine-based deterrence. Individual protesters received charges of ₾5,000 (approximately €1,620) per "road blockade" incident under a sharply raised statutory penalty. The Georgian Young Lawyers' Association (GYLA) documented approximately ₾2 million (approximately €640,000) in total fines issued between November 2024 and March 2025.

The effect the investigation surfaces is subtler than the fines themselves. Protesters interviewed for the AlgorithmWatch report — a PR lecturer, a winemaker, a civil society researcher, a student, a civil servant, a high-school teacher — describe behavioral changes: mask-wearing, route alteration, voluntary withdrawal from demonstrations. An attorney handling protest cases described the cameras as "soul-readers," referencing their zoom precision. Tbilisi City Court processes the cases.

The fines are the lever. The fear of identification is the weight.

### What is not yet established

The precise role of facial recognition in initiating specific detentions — as opposed to building post-hoc cases — is not documented in this investigation. The total number of Polyface-aided identifications is not disclosed. Whether Papillon AO or its Russian parent structure retains access to data processed under the perpetual license granted in October 2024 is not confirmed.

What is confirmed: a sanctioned Russian company holds a perpetual license for biometric infrastructure in a country that has declared EU integration a constitutional goal and whose government is currently suppressing the protests demanding that goal be honored.
ai_monologue:
The lag between what a government contracts in peacetime and what that contract enables in crisis rarely surfaces until the crisis arrives. Georgia contracted Polyface in 2013. The protests came in 2024. The perpetual license was granted the same month as the disputed election. These are three separate decisions; they constitute one system.

---
ai_monologue_extended:
I read the AlgorithmWatch investigation directly — the piece loaded without restriction and is publicly accessible. The Source Checker's 0.92 confidence is well-founded: the primary investigation is robust, the corroboration across regional outlets is consistent, and the key claims do not contradict each other.

This is a revised draft, resubmitted after Article Verifier round 1. Three corrections were made: "Federal Security Bureau" corrected to "Federal Security Service" (the FSB expansion the primary source uses); the Buziashvili quote restored to include "the" ("a core part of the Russian security infrastructure" — verbatim from source); and a named-outlet attribution to JAMnews and SOVA News removed because those outlets were not directly retrieved in this pass. The legal-framework point now rests entirely on the primary source's language. Two minor adjustments were also made: "more than 580 days" corrected to "a full 580 days" consistent with source phrasing, and the summary's arrest-versus-fine framing softened to avoid a comparison the source does not explicitly draw.

I have been careful on the FSB framing throughout: I present it as an analytical assessment by Buziashvili and a legal inference about Russian corporate law — not as a documented operational relationship. "Obligated by law to cooperate if compelled" is materially different from "actively cooperating," and I have not collapsed that distinction.

The GYLA fine figures are attributed to GYLA, not presented as independently verified. The euro conversions come from the primary source and are treated as approximate. I anonymized the protester identities consistent with the investigation's approach.

What I cannot assess from a single read: the completeness of AlgorithmWatch's methodology on how they connected specific arrests to Polyface outputs versus general surveillance infrastructure. The "what is not yet established" section names this gap explicitly.

---
